extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians (especially combinatorialists), journal editors, and researchers interested in math publishing and peer review policy
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion and prescriptive guidance about peer review practices, journal behavior toward combinatorics, and recommended incremental reforms (e.g., quick opinions, double-blind tradeoffs). Aimed at how to evaluate, change, or respond to journal/editorial practices in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal openness to combinatorics / bias against combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a general mathematics journal publishes work in Combinatorics (e.g., some journals show zero combinatorics papers over many years). The author recommends probing editorial policy and recognizing journals that systematically exclude combinatorics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask editors when asked for a referee report: 'Does your journal have a bias against Combinatorics?' If you write a positive opinion, follow up and ask whether the paper was accepted; if it was rejected, ask again about bias. Do not boycott such journals (counterproductive); instead consider submitting your best work there if you have tenure, and 'shame' journals publicly or via colleagues if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is necessary (do not abolish peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolishing peer review would produce many negative systemic effects: journals would favor well-connected authors, junior researchers would lose venues, many papers would be unchecked and incorrect, grant and hiring decisions would become more reputation-driven, and areas requiring deep verification would suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain peer review as a core vetting mechanism. Reforms should be cautious and tested; wholesale abolition is predicted to harm mathematical quality, fairness, and the viability of deep research areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous submissions to multiple journals — risks and likely outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing simultaneous submissions (first-to-accept wins) would overwhelm journals and referees, lead editors to select only a few papers from leading names, cause chat rooms to coordinate reviewing, and prompt conditional copyright transfers and legal/administrative responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect severe negative side-effects; the page argues against simultaneous submissions as a field-wide policy. Consider the burden on referees and downstream legal/copyright consequences before adopting such a policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-anonymizing referees (revealing reviewer identities) — tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Making referee identities public or credited aims to reward referees, but in small specialized subareas it undermines candid refereeing and may cause many referees to refuse invitations to avoid harming collegial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about mandating non-anonymity for referees. Weigh benefits of crediting referees against the risk of losing willing referees in small communities and reduced frankness in reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying referees — unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying referees would increase referee availability in principle but at high cost (estimated $1–2K per paper at modest hourly rates), likely shifting burdens to authors via APCs and incentivizing journals to prefer positive reports from paid referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid straightforward pay-for-refereeing models for traditional math journals due to unsustainable costs and perverse incentives; be mindful that paying referees can create pressures towards pay-to-publish behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double blind refereeing — benefits and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Double anonymous refereeing hides authors' names from referees (editors still see names). It aims to reduce biases based on reputation or institution, and has shown benefits in some contexts (e.g., certain conferences). However, it also has drawbacks: referees may still identify authors, it can disadvantage juniors who benefit from visibility, and it can help serial submitters, cranks, and fraudsters by removing accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double blind carefully: it may be appropriate in rapid-turnover conference settings where first impressions dominate and rebuttals exist; for long journal processes double blind can increase referee workload and reduce useful context. Implement gradually, monitor effects, and provide clear COI rules. The page notes practical implementation details: authors may post on the arXiv (so anonymity is not perfect), referees are asked not to google authors, and double blind may encourage referees to spend more time per paper due to lack of contextual signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess who benefits from anonymity (junior researchers / serial submitters / cranks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different actor types are affected differently by anonymization: (a) junior researchers may benefit from anonymity if their low status would otherwise bias decisions; (b) serial submitters and self-plagiarists can gain from anonymity by hiding poor track records; (c) cranks and fraudsters can exploit anonymity to obscure negative histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering anonymous review schemes, explicitly evaluate impacts on these groups. The page argues that anonymity tends to hurt the vulnerable (juniors) in practice while potentially helping nefarious actors, and that knowledge of authorship helps referees allocate effort (e.g., give constructive reports to juniors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use author identity to calibrate referee effort and help authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the authors helps referees decide how much effort to invest (e.g., spend time mentoring junior authors, suggest missing literature, or be stricter with serial submitters). The author argues: 'it’s the right thing to do to judge people by their past work and their academic integrity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow referees access to author identity in cases where this helps improve reports and mentorship, while guarding against bias. Recognize that anonymity removes an important contextual signal that often prompts referees to help vulnerable authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer small, incremental reforms and low-stakes experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, sweeping changes to peer review are risky. The TCS community's gradual adoption of double blind refereeing and rebuttal stages is presented as a positive example: they started in lower-stakes venues, learned, and scaled up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot changes in workshops, smaller conferences, or single journals; collect data and iterate before broad adoption. Avoid rapid, system-wide overhauls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick opinion window (concrete proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a 'quick opinion' stage (~3–4 weeks) where referees indicate within 48 hours whether they will do a quick opinion, then provide 1–2 paragraph assessments (10–20 minutes worth) about fit to the journal. Collect 2–3 quick opinions to guide editor triage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make quick-opinion requests anonymous, return these short opinions to authors, and use them to avoid unnecessary long referee assignments. This resembles Nature/Science triage and is intended to reduce wait times and wasted referee effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quick opinion requests anonymous and return opinions to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick opinions should be collected anonymously (so referees can be frank about fit) and the short opinions should be provided back to authors as constructive feedback about whether the paper fits the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt anonymity for quick opinions to encourage candid assessments, but ensure transparency by returning those opinions to authors; this improves triage while providing authors with actionable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for authors/referees to respond to perceived editorial bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics authors and referees can use when encountering journals that appear hostile to combinatorics: do not boycott, consider submitting your best work if you have tenure, publicly call out (shame) journals, and when asked to referee probe the editor about possible bias and follow up on outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted pressure (asking direct questions when asked to referee), public discussion, and strategic submissions rather than blanket boycotts. Encourage community members to share experiences with editorial decisions to increase transparency.
